eniac.name: ENIAC and punch cards
eniac.description: Text is numbers. Every character is a pattern of on and off.

visual.body: Programming meant rewiring the machine by hand. No screen, no keyboard: input came as holes in punch cards, results as lamps. Hole or no hole, on or off — every number and every letter was just a pattern of the two.

eniac.insider: Anyone programming with punch cards drew a diagonal line across the top of the deck with a felt-tip pen. If the deck was dropped, the line showed which card went where.

batch.insider: The IBM 704 had sense switches: toggle switches on the console that a running program could read. In FORTRAN that was IF (SENSE SWITCH 3) — the operator could steer a program without stopping it.

unix.name: UNIX
unix.description: A filesystem is a tree. Every file has a path leading to it from the root, /.

unix.insider: Up to the Sixth Edition, the command for changing directory was called chdir. The short cd only arrived in 1979 with the Seventh Edition.

dos.name: IBM PC and MS-DOS
dos.description: Memory is finite. That limit shapes what software can do.

visual.dirVolume: Volume in drive C is AHMADOS
visual.body: Computers arrive on desks. One program at a time, one screen, everything typed. 640 kilobytes of memory — which, contrary to the famous quote nobody can actually source, everyone knew would not be enough for long.

dos.insider: In MS-DOS, F3 brought back the last command line you typed. If you knew that, you never typed a long command twice.

macintosh.name: Macintosh
macintosh.description: Pointing is easier than remembering. Every interface since rests on that idea.

visual.body: 1984, the Apple Macintosh. The first mass-market computer with a mouse and a graphical interface. Instead of memorising commands, you could see something and point at it. Windows, icons, menus, pointer — the vocabulary every interface still speaks today.
visual.screenLabel: Macintosh screen with a menu bar, a window and a mouse pointer
visual.pointerCaption: For the first time: point, not type.

macintosh.insider: The ⌘ symbol on the Command key is Susan Kare's. She found it in a book of symbols: in Sweden it marks places of interest on signs.

win95.name: Windows 95 and dial-up
win95.description: A network needs addresses. Without them, a machine cannot find another machine.

visual.body: 1995, Windows 95 and the modem. The taskbar and the start menu — one place for everything on the machine. And the internet arrives in homes: 56 kbit per second, the phone line occupied. For two computers to find each other, each needs an address. The computer stopped being a solitary machine and became a node in a network.
visual.screenLabel: Windows 95 desktop connecting to the internet over a modem
visual.nodeCaption: A single machine becomes a node in a network.

win95.insider: To see your IP address on Windows 95, you typed winipcfg into Start › Run. Today's ipconfig did not exist there.

cloud.name: Cloud, containers and AI
cloud.description: Programs run isolated from each other, in many places at once.

visual.body: Today. The computer is no longer a single machine. Code runs in containers, sealed off from each other, on servers nobody ever sees — in many data centres at once. And for the first time, a problem can be described in ordinary language and answered. Eighty years from rewiring cables by hand to this.
visual.dashboardLabel: Dashboard of a distributed application with containers, deployment, metrics and regions
response: A container bundles a program with everything it needs to run.
That is why it runs the same everywhere: on your laptop and in any data centre.

cloud.insider: On Linux, only root may open ports below 1024. That is why so many containers listen on port 8080 instead of 80.

eniac.title: The first bug
eniac.invitation: The card reads one letter wrong. Can you find the fault?
eniac.task: The card should spell AHMADREZA, but one column is punched wrong. Punch and clear holes until the name is right.
eniac.hint: Column 5 reads E instead of D. Compare its holes with the table: same zone, different digit.
eniac.answer: In column 5, clear the hole in row 5 and punch row 4. Zone 12 plus digit 4 is D.
eniac.success: AHMADREZA. Every character is just a pattern of hole and no hole, on and off. Your computer still stores that D as 01000100.
eniac.bugNote: The word is older than the story: on 9 September 1947, operators of the Harvard Mark II found a moth in relay 70 and taped it into the logbook as the “first actual case of bug being found”. The logbook is now at the Smithsonian.

batch.title: The queue
batch.invitation: Four jobs are waiting for the machine. In which order does everyone wait the least?
batch.task: Order the jobs so that the total waiting time is as small as possible. Each job waits until every job ahead of it has finished.
batch.hint: Every minute at the front of the queue, everyone behind waits too. So what should run first?
batch.answer: Report (2), Inventory (5), Invoices (15), Payroll (30). Total waiting time: 31 minutes.
batch.success: 31 minutes instead of 115: shortest job first. These are exactly the decisions an operating system makes, so the machine never waits on people.

unix.title: The hidden file
unix.invitation: Somewhere under /home is a hidden file. Can you find it with ls, cd and cat?
unix.task: Find the hidden file and read it with cat. Hidden files start with a dot and only show up with ls -a. Type help for all commands.
unix.hint: Go home with cd /home/ahmadreza and look around with ls. In the projects folder, ls -a helps.
unix.success: Found: /home/ahmadreza/projects/.secret. A filesystem is a tree, and a path is the directions from the root to the file.
unix.help: Commands: pwd  ls  ls -a  cd <path>  cat <file>  clear

dos.title: 640 kilobytes
dos.invitation: The word processor won't start: not enough memory. Can you make room without losing the printer?
dos.task: The word processor needs 384 K of free memory. Unload drivers until it starts. The letter still has to reach the network printer afterwards.
dos.hint: You are 88 K short. Which drivers do you not need to write and print a letter?
dos.answer: Unload the sound driver and the CD-ROM driver, keep the network driver, then start the word processor.
dos.success: The word processor runs, and the printer is reachable. Memory is finite: every driver took a share of the same 640 K, and programs still compete for memory today.
dos.tooBig: Program too big to fit in memory
dos.noNetwork: The word processor runs, but without the network driver the letter cannot find a printer.
dos.memoryLabel: Memory: {used} K of 640 K in use

macintosh.title: Tidy up
macintosh.invitation: For the first time, no command at all: can you tidy the desktop with just the pointer?
macintosh.task: Drag the CV into the Application folder and the old file into the Trash.
macintosh.hint: Press and hold an icon, drag it onto the target and let go. With the keyboard: Space picks up, arrow keys choose the target, Enter drops.
macintosh.answer: Drag CV onto Application, drag Old onto the Trash.
macintosh.success: Tidied up without a single command. Pointing is easier than remembering: in 1981 the same thing took COPY, DEL and a path you had to know by heart.
macintosh.carrying: You are holding {item}. Choose a target.
macintosh.wrongTrash: You still need your CV. Not in the Trash.
macintosh.wrongFolder: The old file does not belong in the application.
macintosh.keyboardHelp: Keyboard: Space picks up, arrow keys choose, Enter drops, Esc cancels.

win95.title: No connection
win95.invitation: The modem is connected, but the network does not answer. Is the address right?
win95.task: Set the IP address, subnet mask and gateway so the PC can reach the router. The router is 192.168.1.1 on network 192.168.1.0 with mask 255.255.255.0. The printer already uses 192.168.1.20.
win95.hint: The gateway has to be inside your own subnet. Compare the first three numbers of your address with the router's.
win95.success: Connected. A network needs addresses: your own, the size of your network – the mask – and the door out, the gateway.

cloud.title: Unreachable
cloud.invitation: portfolio-web is running, but nobody can reach it. Can you find the rule that blocks the way?
cloud.task: The service listens on TCP port 443. The firewall checks its rules top to bottom, and the first match wins. Find the fault and open the right port without opening everything.
cloud.hint: Which rule does a packet for port 443 hit first?
cloud.answer: Rule 2 blocks port 443 before rule 3 is ever checked. Set rule 2 to ALLOW.
cloud.success: Reachable, and everything else stays shut. Every service lives isolated behind its own port, and the firewall decides which door opens.
cloud.wideOpen: Reachable, but now every port is open to the whole internet.
